en: The Sūtra on the Elder Guhagupta, Volume One, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There was an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus; and an assembly of five hundred great bodhisattvas gathered together, each having come from their respective buddha-fields.

They had attained the supernormal power of non-existence and non-action; they had attained the supernormal power of illusory birth; they had attained the accomplishment of pure faith free from dust; they had attained the arising of unobstructed hearing; they had attained deep penetration into all phenomena as being like illusions; they had attained bodies like reflections appearing throughout all buddha-fields; they had attained the ability to turn the wheel of Dharma like an echo; they had attained dream-like wisdom that perceives all worlds in accordance with reality; they had attained the ability to follow the spheres of activity of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Tathāgatas; and they had attained the realm of great wisdom that is unobstructed and unhindered.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Pure Eloquence, Bodhisattva Radiant Flame, Bodhisattva Majestic Treasury, Bodhisattva Immeasurable Light, Bodhisattva Varied Treasury, Bodhisattva Not Abiding in Fixed Buddha-fields, Bodhisattva Moon of the Hero Who Expounds the Buddha-Dharma, Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Accomplishment of the Roots of Goodness through Dhāraṇīs, and Bodhisattva Vairocana’s Diverse Treasury.
Together with these five hundred great bodhisattvas, each of whom had an asaṃkhyeya number of bodhisattvas as their retinue.

At that time, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, elders, householders, as well as various minor kings and followers of diverse non-Buddhist paths, with pure and faithful hearts, honored, revered, and praised the Tathāgata; they made many offerings of excellent garments, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, thus making various offerings to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha accepts their offerings out of a heart of loving-kindness, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, and not out of greed.
Why is this? Because among all fields of merit, the field of the Buddha is the most supreme.

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with immeasurable concentration, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable liberation, and immeasurable knowledge and vision of liberation; as space is boundless and the dharma-realm is boundless, so too is the fivefold dharma-body boundless.
Those who are able to practice relinquishment increase their great merit and accomplish inconceivable fruits of retribution.
Furthermore, he is a guide for all the worlds, skillfully teaching all sentient beings so that they do not abandon the Buddha-dharma;
for those who delight in merit, he serves as an inexhaustible field of blessings; he practices impartial compassion toward all sentient beings and has attained liberation and mastery in omniscience.

At that time, all the non-Buddhist practitioners, such as the Carakas and Parivrājakas, were devoid of faith and gave rise only to craving; furthermore, because they failed to receive honor, offerings, respect, praise, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, they conceived feelings of jealousy.

Seeing that the Buddha’s physical marks and signs were dignified and majestic, and that he had a vast multitude of disciples and followers—whereas the various non-Buddhists possessed none of these—they gave rise to jealousy.
Seeing that the Buddha was endowed with the four types of analytical eloquence and was able to expound all dharmas, while they themselves lacked such eloquence, they gave rise to jealousy.
Seeing that the Buddha received great offerings and gains while they themselves did not, they slandered the Buddha and brought upon him a great ill repute.

Seeing the Buddha’s majestic virtue and the reverence he inspired—such that those who beheld him were struck with awe as if before a great king—they slandered him because they themselves lacked such majesty and virtue.

Seeing that the Buddha was fully endowed with internal and external merits, the thirty-two marks, and all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā), and was beloved by sentient beings, they themselves lacked such qualities and thus gave rise to slander.

He saw that the Buddha was fully endowed with supernatural powers and wisdom, manifesting freely and without obstruction by appearing and disappearing at will; he could transform a single body into many and many bodies into one, his physical power extending sovereignly even unto the Brahma world.

He skillfully knows the various characteristics of all karmic retributions of the past and future; he skillfully knows the mental activities of present sentient beings and preaches the Dharma accordingly: for those with much greed, he teaches the contemplation of impurity; for those with much anger, he teaches the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion; for those with much delusion, he teaches the contemplation of causes and conditions. Sentient beings, having faith and acceptance, distance themselves from greed, anger, and delusion. Yet the various non-Buddhists, lacking such qualities, give rise to jealousy and spread evil reputations about him.

He saw that the Buddha was endowed with the four fearlessnesses and could deliver the definitive Great Lion’s Roar: "If it is thus, one attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya; if it is not thus, there are no fruits of śrāmaṇya. Because the various non-Buddhists lack true knowledge and vision and speak erroneously and perversely, they give rise to slander.

Seeing that the Buddha is fully endowed with great kindness and great compassion, feeling pity for all, and having attained mastery over all sentient beings—perceiving them as clearly as an *āmala* fruit in the palm of one's hand—they themselves lack such qualities and thus give rise to slander.

Seeing that the Buddha receives abundant offerings, respect, and praise, and is revered by devas and humans, they are unable to provide such complete offerings themselves; thus, jealousy arises in their hearts, and they seek to bring him ill repute.
Seeing that the Buddha is thus endowed with various kinds of indestructible merits, yet not possessing them themselves, they give rise to jealousy and slander the Tathāgata.
Those non-Buddhists, their past merit exhausted and new merit not arising, have entered the dense forest wilderness of evil views.
For example, it is like a person who enters a vast wilderness and, having lost the right path, is unable to emerge.

Those non-Buddhists are just like this: separated from wisdom, they cannot escape their various evil views; they do not believe in the True Dharma, they do not make offerings to the Sangha, they have lost their roots of goodness, and they give rise to all manner of evil views. Whatever they say is entirely inverted; they do not believe in the retribution of karma, nor do they understand such dharmas as the twelve links of dependent origination. They wander through the dense forest of evil views rather than the true path, and among all dharmas, they are like those born blind.
At that time, the six heretical teachers and their followers, as well as the naked ascetics and others, all gathered together and went to the Hall of Debate, where they deliberated, saying:

"In the past, before the Śramaṇa Gautama had appeared and while we had not yet seen the Great Śramaṇa, all the people of this Jambudvīpa were subject to us; they believed in and submitted to our teachings, following whatever we desired."

Now that Gautama has appeared in the world, all the people have abandoned our Dharma; they no longer provide us with clothing, food and drink, bedding, or medicinal decoctions, nor do they honor, respect, or praise us, and they do not accept our words.
"What plan should we now devise?
They deliberated further, saying:

"Although the śramaṇa Gautama is fully endowed with merit and wisdom, and is able to convert the kingdom of Aṅga-Magadha so that all its people submit to him, he has been unable to convert this single person, the elder Devarakṣita."

In this city of Rājagṛha, that householder alone does not believe in Gautama; he exclusively accepts my Dharma, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising it, and providing us with robes, food, and drink. He belongs solely to our great assembly of teachers—Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Makkhali Gosāla, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Ajita Keśakambala, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and Akṣapāda Kāśyapa—and no other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have ever before been able to reach his door.

"If our assembly should go to that person's home and they are able to provide various offerings with a sincere heart, it is because that person has today perfected the faculty of faith; they have conceived a supreme confidence toward us that penetrates deep into the very marrow of their bones."
Among the kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and all other people in the city of Rājagṛha, there is no one with such firm faith.

Neither the śramaṇa Gautama nor any of the brāhmaṇas or other heterodox teachers can destroy that person’s faith; we have mastery over him, and whatever he says will certainly be believed and accepted. We should now go to his house and report all these matters to him.

Furthermore, you should instruct them to construct fire-pits beneath each of the seven gates, each pit deep enough to submerge seven men, filled with smokeless *khadira* charcoal embers, with beams made of copper and covered over with grass and earth.
"When Gautama approaches, you must sprinkle water and scatter various flowers; if Gautama steps upon them, he will surely sink and die.
If he does not die, place poison in his food and drink and give it to him to eat."
Having done this, he sent a messenger to invite Gautama to his home for a meal.
"If Gautama is truly all-knowing," [the king thought], "he will certainly not accept the invitation, as he cannot be harmed by fire or poison;
if he is not so, he will undoubtedly accept."
When the non-Buddhist practitioners had formed this plan, they set out together for Rājagṛha. Upon arriving at the house of the great elder Guṇapāla, they stood there waiting in a single file.
At that time, the elder saw the various non-Buddhist practitioners and his heart was filled with great joy; leaping for immeasurable delight, he approached them and paid them homage.
Having prostrated himself, he extensively prepared seats and bedding in various places, urging them to take their seats.
Having taken their seats, they joined their palms, bowed their bodies, and spoke these words:
"We have constantly longed for this; now we have suddenly encountered it.
Excellent! Excellent!"
"Because the devas have thought of me, they have caused all these teachers and great virtuous ones to assemble here, so that I may serve as a field of merit for them.

At that time, when the householder saw that all the non-Buddhist practitioners were seated, he served water in succession, arranged the vessels, provided various kinds of food, and after they had finished eating, he washed their hands.
At that time, the elder sat on a small seat set apart before the couches of the great non-Buddhist ascetics.
When the various non-Buddhist ascetics—such as Luojueduo (Raudhaka), Miduoni (Maitrāyaṇīputra), and Yantuo (Ajita)—saw that the elder was already seated and settled, they spoke these words:
"Great Elder!..."
"When we first gathered in the Great Assembly Hall, we deliberated thus:

'Before the śramaṇa Gautama had appeared, and before we had seen the Great Śramaṇa, all sixteen great kingdoms of Jambudvīpa, such as Aṅga and Magadha, were entirely under our control. They followed our will at their own pleasure, accepted our words with faith, and respectfully made offerings, honoring and praising us, providing us with clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal requisites.'"

Having departed from here, they believe only in that Dharma; they have abandoned us and no longer show us respect, reverence, or provide offerings, nor do they supply us with food, clothing, bedding, or medicinal requisites. The sixteen great kingdoms, such as Aṅga and Magadha, are all now governed by Gautama.
"You alone are my donor; you have accepted my words. No matter what various skillful means the śramaṇa Gautama employs, he will not be able to destroy your faith and acceptance."

Among the sixteen great nations, such as Aṅga and Magadha, there is no one who equals you in believing my words; all the people of those lands, as well as their great kings, likewise believe your words.

"Therefore, we have conceived this plan and deliberated it together with you: you shall now trust me and I shall likewise trust you; whatever discourse we engage in shall be of a single meaning without duality, so that it may not be leaked and known by outsiders."
“Great Householder!

You must now certainly place your full trust in our plan. At each of the seven gates of your residence, you should construct a great fire-pit within every gate, deep enough to submerge seven men. Fill them with smokeless fires of khadira charcoal, using copper for the beams and covering them entirely with reeds and a layer of earth.”
When Gautama was about to arrive, they sprinkled water over it and scattered beautiful flowers upon it, thinking that if Gautama passed over it, he would surely sink into it and die;
if he did not die from burning, they further placed poison within his food. Having performed these acts, they sent word to invite Gautama.
"If he were truly omniscient, he would certainly not accept the invitation; since he accepts it, there is no doubt that he is not omniscient.
At that time, having heard the instructions of the six teachers, the elder was greatly delighted and exclaimed, "Excellent!"
"This plan is most excellent; it accords perfectly with my wishes. I am now capable of providing for all its various requirements; I only pray that the Great Master will not harbor any anxiety.
The six teachers replied, "If this is so, you may prepare everything quickly."
The householder replied: "Excellent!
I shall follow your instructions in every detail. I will immediately prepare a fire pit and poisoned food, and personally invite Gautama. If I do not kill him, there is no one else who can."
"This plan is most essential; our wishes will surely be fulfilled.
Having spoken these words, he leaped for joy and reflected to himself:
"What my teacher has said is most excellent!"
"Excellent!

At that time, the various teachers of the non-Buddhist paths congratulated themselves, thinking that what they had previously taught was now entirely consistent with the present. They spoke these words of praise:

"We have taught him to abandon wholesome deeds and perform evil karma; we have taught him to abandon non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and to establish himself on a path of intolerance toward greed, hatred, and delusion. Even such irrational teachings he is still able to follow."
"Excellent!
Householder, you truly believe my words.
Uttering these words of great joy, some sang and others whistled, and each took their leave to return to their respective places.

At that time, there was a son of the elder Guṇapāla named Candraprabha, who was sixteen years of age. His physical appearance was upright and handsome, his features were foremost among men, and his body possessed twenty-eight marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Sentient beings who beheld him could never tire of gazing upon him. Having already made offerings to past Buddhas and planted various roots of virtue, he had heard and received the True Dharma from many Buddhas and purified his Brahma-conduct in the presence of eight hundred million Buddhas. He was wise, of sharp faculties, courageous, and firm; he was endowed with eloquence, straightforward, and without guile. His mind and speech were in accord, and he attained the Buddha-recollection Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). In the presence of all Buddhas, he constantly maintained a heart of joy, and within the True Dharma, he always possessed a heart of rapture and delight.

With a mind free from timidity, they attain the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and unshakable faith; their minds are free from the net of doubt regarding all dharmas. They are able to provide the Sangha with offerings of exquisite clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; they are skillful in preaching the Dharma and attain dhāraṇīs, reaching the stage of non-retrogression and attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Within enlightenment, they attain an inconceivable body and mind;

among all sentient beings, they attain a great compassion that is indestructible. They constantly and diligently teach and transform all sentient beings, never retreating from their vow for omniscience, and are able to destroy all demonic adversaries and subdue all non-Buddhists.

They have attained wisdom and skillful means, and have attained profound wisdom; they can relinquish things like clouds, maintain pure precepts, possess patience like the earth, and are firm in their diligence.

With the mind undisturbed amidst all phenomena, one is able to practice wisdom and perceive all dharmas as they truly are; one attains the nourishment of the Dharma within all phenomena, makes offerings to the Buddhas with the most supreme faith, and gives rise to trust and delight in the various merits of the Buddhas, while maintaining pure compassion.

They give rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings; their faith is as firm and immovable as a mountain of diamond; they attain the wisdom of non-forgetful mindfulness in its various aspects, and are able to receive all dharmas and reach the further shore.

With wisdom, they understand the skillful means of all Buddha-dharmas; their power of merit and virtue is indestructible; abiding in the four analytical eloquences, their minds are free from timidity; and toward their parents, they recognize their kindness and repay it with gratitude.

They attain the most supreme mind regarding all Buddha-dharmas and constantly expound the merits of the Buddhas for the sake of sentient beings. Whether seeing or hearing the supernatural powers of the Buddhas, their minds never feel satiated. They are skillfully able to gather those who possess wisdom and can explain the spheres of all Buddhas; they are fully capable of lecturing upon and expounding all Buddha-dharmas.

This son of a householder has accomplished such merits as these; he is a vessel for the Dharma of such immeasurable proportions that, were one to speak extensively of his infinite praises, they could never be exhausted.
This youth Candracchattra, knowing that his father, the householder, had placed faith in non-Buddhist paths and intended to harm the Tathāgata, went immediately to his mother and said to her:
"Mother, do you know this now?"

The father’s mind was inverted; having received the teachings of external paths, he lost his original mind. He felt great joy toward what he had obtained from those external paths and gave rise to deep reverence and faith. These external path practitioners themselves create the karma for the three evil realms, and they also cause their father to create the karma for the three evil realms.
Mother, do not now accept your father’s words of false view to slander the Buddha.

Why is this? It is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; throughout the long course of kalpas, one may encounter him only once in a single kalpa, ten kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, or even after an inexpressible number of kalpas.
The names of the Buddhas are yet beyond hearing, let alone being seen!

The Buddha can purify the minds of all sentient beings; he is fully endowed with supernatural powers and wisdom, possessing thorough and unimpeded comprehension. He is skillfully able to teach and transform all sentient beings; his conduct is without obstruction, and among those who have attained the three gates of liberation, the Buddha is the most supreme.

In a single moment of thought, he knows all phenomena; the Tathāgata dwells skillfully within all phenomena. The Tathāgata can know the places where all sentient beings are born; the Buddha’s words of truth serve as a witness for all sentient beings, able to eliminate the various enemies and the physical and mental afflictions of sentient beings, remaining without attachment to any sensory realms.
Mother, you should believe in the Buddha; do not believe the false and deceptive words of the six teachers.
Out of my reverence for you and to repay your kindness, I offer these words to you. Why is this?
My mother carried me in her womb for ten full months, enduring great suffering and distress; when she gave birth to my body, she was half-dead and half-alive, fainting and reviving again and again.
I have never forgotten this kindness, and even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, it could never be repaid.

My heart always aspires that I may go together with my mother to see hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas; it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to hear the teachings of all Buddhas; it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to visit all the dwelling places of Bodhisattvas; it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to visit all the pure places where the Buddha-dharma is established by Bodhisattvas; it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to visit all places of indestructible, pure faith; it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to visit all places where the work of a Buddha is performed; it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to visit all places where offerings of incense, flowers, robes, bedding, and medicinal decoctions are made to the Triple Gem; it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to visit all places where noble beings practice the Dharma; and it always aspires that I may go together with my mother to visit all places where the faculty of faith is perfected, free from inversion, and leading to Nirvana.
At that time, her mother Candrābhā said to Candraprabhā:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
I have been fortunate to hear your teaching.
You are truly possessed of great compassion; you have conceived deep pity for your parents and guided them toward virtuous deeds like a great leader.

You are likewise so now, and all that you have taught is being faithfully accepted. For the sake of purifying my own mind and for the sake of bringing peace and security to all sentient beings, I now resolve to generate the bodhicitta—the vast mind, the supreme mind, the immeasurable mind, the joyful mind—and give rise to a pure mind. Among all phenomena, I shall attain a mind free from doubt, a mind free from inversion, and a mind endowed with perfect faith.

Within the community of monks, there are those who possess liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, capable of destroying all afflictions and fetters; one should therefore give rise to pure faith toward them and offer them worship and respect.

The virtues of the Buddha are immeasurable, the practices of the Buddha are immeasurable, and the realm of the Buddha is immeasurable; the sublime Dharma he teaches is likewise immeasurable, and his benefit to sentient beings is likewise immeasurable.
"As you have said, the virtues of the Buddha are boundless; I am currently without wisdom to fully describe the Buddha's merits.
Candraprabha!

I always have faith in the Buddha and never give rise to an evil thought toward him. You are truly my great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), for you are able to speak to me of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues; even if one were to speak of the Buddha’s merits for immeasurable thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one would never reach satiety nor find their limit."
At that time, Candragarbha spoke these verses to his son:
"For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, the name of a Buddha is difficult to hear, let alone to behold.
That you are able to give rise to supreme faith in the Buddha—such faith is truly difficult to obtain."
I now have faith in the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues, which are impossible even to hear, let alone to see with one's own eyes;
that you have now been born into my home, I now behold you as a true guide.
You have enabled my mind to attain pure faith in the inconceivable teachings of all Buddhas;
you are now like my parents, and like the Buddhas who have brought me into their own family.
Just as parents take their child away, leading them to the stainless realm of all Buddhas,
we could not repay your kindness today even in immeasurable thousands of millions of kalpas.
You are truly my good spiritual friend; throughout all lifetimes, you have always been my pure guide.
You have caused me to dwell securely in the most excellent mindfulness, so that I possess certain faith in the Buddha without any doubt.
Forever emerging from the three evil realms, Always dwelling securely in the human and heavenly paths—
Not only is he my spiritual friend, But he is also the spiritual friend of all sentient beings.
If one still desires to deliver other sentient beings, how much more so one's own kin and parents?
One can cause all members of the family and their relatives to break all bonds of enmity,
further distance themselves from the three evil realms, and transcend to abide in the paths of gods and humans.

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is exceedingly rare; having passed through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have now been able to come to be born into my family. Such a rarity is likewise difficult to encounter;
you are truly a great man (mahāpuruṣa), who is well able to skillfully expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
You are now truly a child of all Buddhas, always giving rise to joyful faith in the Buddha.
Who has now granted me this rare son, who is now born into my family?
My son Candraprabha is most extraordinary; he is always able to praise all Buddhas.

At that time, within the household of the elder Guṇaprabha, the one thousand court ladies heard these verses spoken by Lady Candrāvatī and the youth Candraprabha; they were all filled with immense joy and leaped for joy beyond measure, and with one voice they praised them, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
It is inconceivable, truly inconceivable!
That the moonlight-like *pudgala* has been born into my family—such a man is difficult even to hear of, let alone to behold!

Wherever such a person is born—whether in a city, town, or village of Jambudvīpa—if anyone sees, hears, associates with, or makes offerings to them, and even shares a seat or conversation with them, shall forever be free from the evil realms; how much more so for those born into their own family who do not fail to receive benefit?
"Your parents and kinsmen shall be led away from the evil realms.
At that time, after the elder Guhagupta had sent the non-Buddhists away, he departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, where he went in person to invite the Buddha.

From afar he saw the World-Honored One, adorned with inconceivable marks and signs, his six sense faculties stilled; having attained the most excellent *dhyāna* and *śamatha*, and the most supreme, foremost *dhyāna* and *śamatha*; guarding his sense faculties like a tamed great dragon, like the waters of a vast lake, pure and unclouded; emitting immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of radiant flames; his majestic virtue and solemn deportment were difficult to behold, yet those who saw him were filled with joy.
When the householder Guṇapāla had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they exchanged various gentle words of greeting and inquiry, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will have compassion for me and accept my offerings tomorrow."
The Buddha, knowing that the time had come for the elder to be transformed, accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Having understood this, the elder’s heart was filled with joy; he prostrated himself, took his leave, and descended from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, entering the city of Rājagṛha to go to the dwellings of the six teachers.
Having arrived, he spoke these words:
"The śramaṇa Gautama and his assembly have already accepted my invitation; by this, it is known that he is not omniscient."

When the various non-Buddhists heard these words, their hearts were filled with joy; they leaped for exceeding delight, feeling immeasurable gratitude and a sense of fulfillment that pervaded both body and mind. They spoke to the elder, saying:
"You may now return home and quickly prepare the fire pit and poisoned food as previously described, so that your purpose may be accomplished."
At that time, the elder immediately returned home and commanded his family members to prepare for this matter.
Then the son, Candraprabha, seeing his father give rise to the intention to commit an evil deed, felt deep distress in his heart and admonished his father, saying:
"This matter is inauspicious; do not create unwholesome karma against the Buddha."

Why is this? Because the Buddhas are indestructible; among all devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, none can destroy one who commits acts of malice or rebellion against the Tathāgata. No swords or blades can wound or ruin them, and no fierce fires can burn or harm them. Even if the fires of hell were to burn them, they would not feel even warmth, let alone human fire.

Just as when the kalpa comes to an end and seven suns appear simultaneously, filling the great trichiliocosm with blazing fires that burn up to the Brahma Heaven and the Iron Ring Mountains, they still cannot burn even a single robe of the Buddha; how much less could this tiny fire-pit possibly burn or harm the Tathāgata? Such a thing is impossible.

Even if a thunderbolt-fire as vast as Mount Sumeru were set ablaze, it could not reach the traces of the Tathāgata’s movements or his four modes of deportment; how much less could this fire-pit burn or harm him?
The Buddha is able to extinguish all the great poisons found in the entire world, such as the waters of the great ocean; how much more so could a small poison placed within food possibly harm him?
"Even if poisonous medicine were as high as the Snowy Mountains, the Buddha’s eye would naturally cause it to vanish; how much less could this poisoned food possibly cause harm?

'I pray that my father will not act like a small person by creating various evil karmas and establishing causes and conditions for being far from the Buddha; only those who possess all merit and virtue are able to draw near.'"
I pray that you, Father, do not give rise to thoughts of malice, hostility, or hatred toward the Buddha; for the nature of the minds of all sentient beings is pure.
Do not give rise to a defiled and turbid mind of affliction;
do not join hands with the heterodox, nor compare a tiny mustard seed to Mount Sumeru, or the water in a cow’s footprint to the great ocean.
Do not seek to pervade the entirety of empty space with the small web of a spider;
do not seek to move Mount Sumeru with the strength of a single speck of dust;
do not seek to contain Mount Cakravāḍa within a single pore.
Do not seek to fill the trichiliocosm with a single grain of sand. Why?

Because the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and unobstructed; because it transcends all worldly obstructive phenomena; because the Buddha is endowed with the ten powers that cannot be destroyed by any other power; and because the Tathāgata possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa, such that no evil committed by any sentient being can cause him harm.

“The Tathāgata is firm and indestructible; the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, dwelling in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The Tathāgata has no grasping, being free from attachment among all phenomena. The Tathāgata has no dependence within the three periods of time. The Tathāgata is quiescent and has no location. The Tathāgata is supremely tranquil, free from all afflictions and fevers. The Tathāgata is extinguished and is the most preeminent among all beings. The Tathāgata is peerless, surpassing all metaphors. The Tathāgata’s three karmas proceed in accordance with wisdom. The Tathāgata is pure, practicing the Dharma free from defilement. The Tathāgata is valiant and heroic, destroying all Māras and non-Buddhists.

The Tathāgata possesses inexhaustible power through his eloquence. The Tathāgata is well-tamed, for he is able to bring the untamed to subjugation; the Tathāgata is well-quiescent, for he is able to bring the unquiescent to extinction.”
The water of the Tathāgata’s wisdom can sprinkle away the various afflictions of sentient beings;
it can cause those with many afflictions to become free from affliction.
“The Tathāgata is the most honored among all sentient beings, for he has attained the crown of omniscience.”
The Tathāgata is a great cloud capable of raining upon all, for the rain of Dharma is inexhaustible;
the Tathāgata is able to fulfill the mental activities of all sentient beings;
and the Tathāgata has attained non-deceptive wisdom, whereby he knows the mental activities of sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Because the Tathāgata can reveal the past roots of goodness and practices of all sentient beings;
because the Tathāgata can extinguish the flow of afflictions of all sentient beings;
and because those who behold the Tathāgata never tire of gazing upon him.
“Because the Buddha is peerless among all bodhisattvas;
because the Tathāgata is able to exhaust all afflictions;
because the Tathāgata is able to sever the torrential river of all afflictions.”
The Tathāgata fulfills great compassion for all sentient beings and is able to protect them; thus, those who see him all attain peace and security, and it is not in vain.
The Tathāgata, the Sugata, is like a lion king, for he has no fear regarding any world.
The Tathāgata is supreme among all worlds, for the sentient beings of the three periods of time cannot defile him.
Because no power or sovereignty in any world can destroy it;
because the Tathāgata has reached the ultimate pinnacle of all phenomena throughout the entire dharma-realm;
and because the Tathāgata is quiescent and free from conceptual proliferation.
The Tathāgata knows all and sees all, for he is able to know the phenomena of the past, future, and present.

Even before attaining bodhi, he had already foreknown that at the time of his attainment of bodhi, there would be a great elder named Śrīgupta in the city of Rājagṛha who, with a turbid and evil mind, intended to kill the Tathāgata by means of a fire pit and poisoned food; he also knew that through the causes and conditions of this evil mind, [Śrīgupta] would be able to attain the most supreme, pure, and excellent faith and abandon his turbid mind.
The Tathāgata is able to teach and transform all sentient beings who commit evil or perform good, causing them to create the causes and conditions for unexcelled bodhi.
"I pray that my father will relinquish all evil thoughts, poisonous malice, and sinful minds."

Why is this? It is like, for example, there being one person who makes offerings to the great earth and another person who burns and cuts the great earth; toward these two people, [the earth] provides benefit without any distinction.
The Buddha is also like this: toward those who offer him worship and toward those who strike or revile him, he—by virtue of his original vows—acts as the causal condition for all to attain the Way.

Therefore, the Tathāgata plants the roots of goodness for all sentient beings and is the most supreme and foremost among all fields of merit. If there are those who make offerings to the Buddha, they will certainly be able to transcend the three realms; the Buddha is the great spiritual friend of all sentient beings.
“Father, if you now give rise to an evil mind toward the Buddha, you will lose yourself and burn yourself, heading toward hell to undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
However, the body of the Tathāgata cannot be destroyed; neither any of the non-Buddhists nor any sentient beings can destroy it.”

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already departed from the fierce fires of the three poisons and has attained liberation within ignorance; he has attained the wisdom of the three periods of time, enabling him to know the past and present of sentient beings, to leave behind all transgressions and attain all blessings, and to perfect the roots of all virtues.

Therefore, father, you should give rise to deep faith and joy; do not conceive thoughts of enmity toward the Tathāgata; do not follow the deluded teachings of external paths and distance yourself from the Buddha; do not harbor a rebellious or malicious mind toward the Buddha, nor a heart of resentment; do not harbor thoughts of harm toward the Tathāgata, who is your true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); lest you fall into the three miserable realms and later feel regret.
At that time, the elder Guṇaprabha said to Candraprabha:

"If, as you have said, the Buddha possesses immeasurable merit and is an omniscient one who knows the minds of others, why did he not know that I had prepared a fire pit and poisoned food with an evil intent, yet still accepted my invitation?"
At that time, Candraprabha said to his father:
"The Buddha is truly all-knowing and truly all-seeing; he perceives and knows all the evil thoughts within you, and he also knows that you shall be tamed because of these evil thoughts."

The Buddha’s wisdom is the greatest; he possesses the sovereign power of awakening and perfect knowledge. It is because he wishes to eliminate his father’s evil mind that he now accepts his father’s invitation, and not for the sake of food.

Father, you should contemplate the Buddha’s great adornments and the Buddha’s great supernormal powers. It is because the Buddha, out of great compassion, desires to bring liberation to your evil and turbid mind that he has come here;
it is because he desires to cause those with evil objects of attachment to cultivate roots of goodness;
and it is because he desires to bring about the liberation of your body.
Because they have attained self-mastery;
because they desire to transform the darkened mind into a luminous mind;
and because they desire to transform the black mind into a white mind.
It is because he wishes to transform a turbid mind into a pure mind;
because he desires to cause his father—who had faith in the evil and turbid teachings of non-Buddhists—to become greatly purified;
and because he wishes to eliminate the mass of suffering within the entire triple world.
"If my father does not believe that the Buddha possesses various great supernormal powers, he shall know for himself tomorrow morning.
Then, after this night had passed, the elder Śrīgupta, at dawn on the following morning, dispatched a messenger to invite the Buddha, saying:
"Speak to the Great Śramaṇa as I have told you:"
“The requisites are prepared; please know that now is the time.
At that time, the messenger left the city of Rājagṛha and went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [The requisites are prepared.]”
"Householder Guṇapāla has finished preparing the food; may the Buddha know that it is time.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Put on your robes, take up your bowls, and go to the home of the great householder Guṇapāla to accept his invitation for a meal."
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “So be it;
we shall receive your instruction.
They then returned each to their own quarters, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to where the Tathāgata was, standing each to one side.

At that time, the Tathāgata, like a great lion king exerting his prowess, from his four tusks—each tusk emitting hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light in various colors—and each tooth likewise;
from his two hands, two arms, two shoulders, and the *uṣṇīṣa* on his crown, each emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light in various colors;
and from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, he further emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of rays of light in various colors.
His entire body also emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of various colored rays of light;
from the syllable *De* upon his chest, he again emitted immeasurable tens of millions of nayutas of various colored rays of light;
and from his navel wheel, he again emitted a ray of light named "Destroyer of All Darkness," with hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of various lights as its retinue.

Furthermore, by means of his supernormal power, he emitted immeasurable light; this light shone everywhere throughout all Buddha-fields in the eastern direction, and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, shining everywhere throughout all Buddha-fields in the same manner.

At that time, to the east, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, there was a world named Jambūdhvaja-prabhāsa. In that land, there was a buddha named Maitreyeśvararāja, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who was currently preaching the Dharma.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Sumeruprabha, surrounded by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) retinue; furthermore, there were ten thousand bodhisattvas all bearing the same name, Sumeruprabha, who together set out toward the Sahā world.

Throughout the various countries he passed through, he raised great clouds of precious jewels and rained down all kinds of treasures. Upon reaching Vulture Peak Mountain and arriving at the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet. He had come to the Buddha’s presence for the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of reverent offering, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Guṇapāla in the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, to the south, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, there was a buddha-field named Fire Flavor. There, the Buddha known as King of the Well-Abiding Jewel Banner, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.

In that buddha-field, there was a bodhisattva named Samantaguṇatejoraśmirāja, along with ten thousand other bodhisattvas, all likewise named Samantaguṇatejoraśmirāja. Each of these bodhisattvas was surrounded by a retinue of asaṃkhyeya followers who paid him respectful homage. Together they set out toward the Sahā world, emitting immeasurable asaṃkhyeya rays of light that filled every land they passed through. For the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of paying respectful offerings, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Śrīgupta, they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, to the west, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world-systems, there was a Buddha-field named Sarvavyūha. There dwelt a Buddha named Sarvavyāpīprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there, teaching the Dharma.

In that buddha-field there was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabhāmegharāja, and there were ten thousand other bodhisattvas all sharing the same name, Samantaprabhāmegharāja. Each of these bodhisattvas was accompanied by a retinue of asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas. Together they respectfully surrounded him as they traveled toward the Sahā world. As they passed through various lands, they raised clouds of various precious flowers and rained down various precious flowers, surpassing all offerings made by devas and humans. They came to the place where the Buddha was—Śrīgupta (translated in the Sui language as "Virtue-Protected")—in order to see the Buddha, to pay him respectful homage and offerings, to see the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Guṇapāla.
The Sūtra on the Elder Guhagupta Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Upper;
The Sūtra on the Elder Guhagupta Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty.
At that time, to the north, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems, there was a buddha-land named Jvālāloka.
There, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Guṇagaṇaśikhara-vikrīḍitarāja was currently residing and preaching the Dharma.

In that buddha-world, there was a bodhisattva named Rocana-Prabhāsa-Mahāraśmi, and there were also ten thousand other bodhisattvas, all bearing the same name, Rocana-Prabhāsa-Mahāraśmi. Each of these bodhisattvas was accompanied by a retinue of asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas, who respectfully surrounded them as they traveled toward the Sahā world. As they passed through various lands, they emitted pure incense-flames of agallochum; the fragrance universally perfumed each of the buddha-worlds of the ten directions, extending ten times asaṃkhyeya-fold beyond those worlds and surpassing all the adornments of devas and humans. They came to the place where the Buddha was for the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of making offerings, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Śrīgupta (in Sanskrit, Śrīgupta).

At that time, to the northeast, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world-systems, there was a Buddha-field named Sarvaratnavyuha. There, the Buddha named Dharmeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, currently dwelt and taught the Dharma.

In that realm there was a bodhisattva named Free from Obstructions and Supernatural Powers (*Vighnāntara-vinivartana-ṛddhi*), who was accompanied by ten thousand other bodhisattvas all bearing the same name, each with an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) retinue of bodhisattvas. They respectfully surrounded him as they journeyed toward the Sahā world. Throughout the lands they passed, they praised all Buddhas with voices perfected through roots of goodness purified over ten million *koṭis* of kalpas. They raised great clouds of Dharma and rained down a multitude of Dharma rains until they reached the presence of the Buddha. It was for the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of making offerings, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Śrīgupta that they came to the Buddha’s abode.

At that time, to the southeast, past as many world-systems as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, there was a world named Universal Adornment. In that realm dwelt a Buddha named Unobstructed Radiance Flame Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who was currently preaching the Dharma.

In that realm there was a bodhisattva named Samantābhāsa-viśuddhacandra, and there were ten thousand other bodhisattvas all bearing the same name. Each of these bodhisattvas was accompanied by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas as they surrounded him from front and back, proceeding toward the Sahā world. As they passed through various lands, they emitted a radiance adorned with various jewels, and networks of golden jewel bells completely covered and filled all of space. Their sound was as subtle and wondrous as the voices of a hundred buddhas; they came to the presence of the Buddha in order to see him, to make offerings to him, to see the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Guṇarakṣa.

At that time, to the southwest, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, there was a world named Covered with Golden Nets. In that world dwelt a Buddha, named King of Supreme Conduct (Vijayacāra-rāja) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who is currently present and preaching the Dharma.

In that world, there was a bodhisattva named Mṛdusvaravikrīḍita, along with ten thousand other bodhisattvas all named Mṛdusvaravikrīḍita, each accompanied by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) retinue of bodhisattvas. They traveled to the Sahā world, and as they passed through various lands, they raised clouds of precious parasols that filled the void. Each bodhisattva carried a parasol, and every precious canopy had pendants made of pearls, pure and distinct like the light of a Buddha. For the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of making offerings, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Śrīgupta, they came to where the Buddha was.

At that time, to the northwest, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems, there was a world named Universal Entry. There, the Buddha known as Unobstructed Moon Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, currently dwells and expounds the Dharma.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Immeasurable Musical Sound, and there were ten thousand other bodhisattvas all bearing the same name, Immeasurable Musical Sound. Together with an immeasurable number of asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas as their retinue, they respectfully surrounded him and proceeded toward the Sahā world. As they passed through each of the various lands, every single bodhisattva emitted from every one of his pores the sounds of asaṃkhyeya musical instruments, singing praises of all the Buddha-dharmas. For the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of making offerings, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Śrīgupta, they came to the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, below this world, past as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world-systems, there was a Buddha-world named Jewel Lotus Well-Abiding. The Buddha there was named Lamp of the World for All Sentient Beings, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Samantameghaguṇa, and there were ten thousand other bodhisattvas who shared the same name. Each of these bodhisattvas was accompanied by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) number of bodhisattvas as his retinue. Together they respectfully surrounded him and proceeded toward the Sahā world. As they passed through various lands, they raised clouds of precious lotuses and rained down flowers of infinite varieties and colors, adorning incalculable buddha-fields. For the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of making offerings, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Śrīgupta, they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, above this world, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, there was a Buddha-world named Variegated Flower Banner (*Vicitrapuṣpadhvaja*). In that realm dwelt a Buddha named King of the Swift Array of Various Jewels (*Nānāratnavikurvaṇarāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who currently resides there teaching the Dharma.

In that world there was a bodhisattva named Darśanam-anarthaka (He Whose Sight is Not in Vain), and there were ten thousand other bodhisattvas all bearing the same name. Each of these bodhisattvas was accompanied by a retinue of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattvas. Together they respectfully surrounded him and proceeded toward the Sahā world. As they passed through various lands, they raised clouds of sandalwood-flavored incense and rained down incense of manifold flavors, filling incalculable buddha-fields. For the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of making offerings, for the sake of seeing the youth Candraprabha, and out of compassion for the elder Śrīgupta, they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

Thus, all these Bodhisattvas of Infinite Supreme Bodies from every direction and non-direction, each coming from their own lands and Buddha-fields, manifested great majestic power, radiant colors, and forms as they gathered together.

From Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa up to the Summit of Existence, and throughout the entire trichiliocosm, all were brilliantly illuminated; these bodhisattvas, having perfected the adornments of bodhisattva practice, shone with pure radiance, their minds abiding nowhere.

In inconceivable asaṃkhyeya Buddha-fields, they are able to transcend them and purely cultivate the brahma-faring in the presence of the Buddhas; they increase their vows, wisdom, and skillful means, and they never regress from inconceivable samādhis. Should anyone see or hear of these bodhisattvas, or draw near to them, it shall all be not in vain.

At that time, when the World-Honored One saw that the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions, together with their retinues of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattvas, had each arrived from their own buddha-fields to assemble here, he immediately unbound his cross-legged posture, desiring to proceed to the home of the great elder Śrīgupta.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways and eighteen manners:

it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere; it shuddered, shuddered everywhere, and shuddered equally everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere.

At that time, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lotus flowers sprang up from the earth; there were incalculable fragrances, incalculable lights, incalculable flames, incalculable precious flower-garlands, incalculable flower-stems made of various mani-jewels, incalculable flower-pedestals made of various mani-jewels, incalculable Vairocana-treasuries, and incalculable qualities and colors that could not be exhausted.

At that time, the World-Honored One stepped upon the precious lotuses and adjusted his robes. By means of his supernormal powers, he manifested hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lotus petals, which sprang up from the earth in various colors: their stalks were made of blue lapis lazuli and the treasury of virtue; their filaments were made of the jewel of the flavor of ambrosia; their calyxes were made of the true maṇi-treasury jewel; and from the fragrance of dragon-firm sandalwood, hundreds of thousands of flames issued forth.

In this manner, rows of lotuses were arranged in succession from Vulture Peak Mountain to the house of the great elder Guṇapāla, such that precious flowers completely covered and filled the entire space.
Furthermore, by means of his supernormal power, he universally emitted light from all parts of his body, illuminating all Buddha-fields in the eastern direction;
likewise, for all Buddha-fields in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, the radiance shone forth in the same manner.

All the palaces, all the houses, the inner and outer city walls, the streets, the barriers, and even the spaces beneath the beds within this city of Rājagṛha were completely illuminated, such as no people had ever seen before.

At that time, the Tathāgata, surrounded and attended with reverence by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and great arhats, who filled the void and stepped upon precious lotus flowers, descended from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and entered the city of Rājagṛha, arriving at the home of the great elder Guṇapāla.

When the Buddha descended, the Naga King Anavatapta, together with five hundred naga sons of immeasurable varieties of colors and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of other naga kings, released immeasurable clouds of incense and rained down immeasurable showers of incense, attending upon the Tathagata.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings attended upon and escorted the World-Honored One, raining down immeasurable clouds of jewels that were scattered along the path.
On both sides of the road, they fashioned railings made of the seven treasures, which were filled with all manner of exquisite adornments.
All such celestial kings, all dragon kings, and all night...
The King of Yakṣas, all the Gandharva Kings, Asura Kings, Garuḍa Kings, Mahoraga Kings, Kiṃnara Kings, Brahmā, Mahābrahmā, and Abhāsvara Brahmā,
surrounded by immeasurable thousands of koṭis of nayutas of retinues, respectfully encircled him, singing hymns and offering praise.
They uttered praises— true praises, most true praises, non-erroneous praises, non-dual praises, supreme praises,
most supreme praises, joyful praises, and praises in accordance with the Buddha’s Dharma—
filling the entirety of space with such eulogies.
Furthermore, with such forms of reverent offering, superior offering, most excellent offering, incalculable offering, and offerings surpassing the incalculable.
Soaring through the void, they attended upon the Tathāgata as he entered the city of Rājagṛha and arrived at the gate of the elder’s residence.

The Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Asura Kings, the Yakṣa Kings, and others likewise followed along the road from the great city of Rājagṛha, standing in attendance until they reached the gate of the great elder Śrīgupta.

At that time, the youth Candraprabha, seeing the Buddha’s radiance and great supernormal powers, as well as the eighteen signs by which the great earth shook, was filled with great joy and a serene mind. His faculties were blissful and his entire body was suffused with satisfaction. Having given rise to this joy, he ascended a seven-storied tower, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation toward his father, and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha has risen from his cross-legged seat, And set forth, desiring to come here.
Fearless like a lion, He has now arrived at this place.”
This Nārāyaṇa who has come here, the indestructible Honored One among Two-legged Beings, has shattered Māra and his retinue and risen at that Bodhi tree.
This one who has come is like a vajra; nothing at all can destroy him.
Yet they are able to destroy all those of wrong views and external paths.
Just as a mighty warrior can defeat all enemies,
so too can compassion scatter and extinguish the afflictions of arrogance.
This arrival is difficult to destroy; it overcomes others and transcends all in excellence.
The Great Teacher of Wisdom is able to rescue and deliver all.
This arrival cannot be killed; it cannot be burned by any fires.
The Tathāgata has already transcended death; no manifold poisons can harm him.
This Great Man who has come here is the supreme teacher;
his body is the most excellent in the three realms, and none can equal it.
With perfectly rounded shoulders and profound wisdom, together with the compassionate assembly of noble ones,
he is unsurpassed among all classes of sentient beings.
Endowed with every mark of physical excellence, he is adorned with the eighty minor characteristics.
The radiance of their bodies illuminates all; disciplined, pure, and free from outflows, they come through the void by means of this vehicle.
Free from transgression and without attachment, they do not dwell in mixed perceptions or contemplations, but abide eternally in the path of reality.
Coming from the inexhaustible, he is able to extensively expound all dharmas;
the inconceivable wheel of Dharma, its various distinctions, he knows.
This one who has come is the All-Knowing One, able to awaken to all dharmas.

Possessing the ten powers, great compassion, and so forth, And abiding securely in the four analytical eloquences, He comes here to appear not in vain; He can bestow peace and security upon the multitude.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, It is difficult even to hear his name, let alone to behold him.
This one who has come is a tamer of dragons, a manly lion;
out of inconceivable compassion for the masses, he has practiced for immeasurable eons.
This one who has come is a master of sovereignty; no sentient being can obstruct him.
The Great Compassionate Guide, who can fulfill the wishes of those who seek;
this arriving spiritual friend dwells in the most supreme realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
boundless as space, awakening to all dharmas in a single thought-moment.
Having come here, free from duality, you have reached the further shore of all phenomena;
within the ground of signlessness, you have arrived at the most supreme and excellent awakening.
Having come here, you are able to purify the two kinds of giving: that of material wealth and that of the Dharma.
In past lives, he sacrificed his body and life out of compassion for sentient beings.
This Guide who has come here bestows peace and security upon all;
having practiced for immeasurable eons, it was for the sake of seeking Bodhi.
With a mind of equal great wisdom, one constantly cultivates excellence within the Dharma;
regarding enemies and kin as no different, the mind is pure and free from discrimination.
Like a lion’s majestic leap, one delivers sentient beings through the power of the supernatural faculties.
Throughout all infinite lands, his radiance shines everywhere;
though one were to praise the Tathāgata’s virtues for accumulated eons,
a single pore could never be exhausted, let alone his entire body.

At that time, the youth Candraprabha’s younger sister, Candrottarā, who was of upright and beautiful form, heard the youth Candraprabha recite verses in praise of the Buddha; her body and mind were filled with joy. Furthermore, seeing the Tathāgata’s radiant brilliance and because her heart rejoiced at the great supernormal power that caused the great earth to tremble, she joined her ten fingers in palms-together gesture before her father and spoke these verses again:
“As my brother Candraprabha has praised, The Tathāgata’s manifold virtues Are found nowhere else in all the worlds;
I pray that my father will believe and accept them.”
Do not believe the words of non-Buddhists; with minds constantly harboring anger and envy, they give rise to malice toward the One of Ten Powers.
Through evil thoughts, they lose their virtuous mind.
Because they do not understand the Buddha-dharma, they do not believe or accept it when it is taught.
By committing evil, one loses the path of goodness; before the Buddha, one cannot explain this away.
Accepting the words of those with false views, one shall fall into the various evil realms;
because of jealousy, delusion, and turbidity, one then loses the virtuous mind.
With evil views as the conditions for the three poisons, craving thus increases;
because of this inverted and deluded mind, one remains far removed from all Buddha-dharmas.
For immeasurable thousands of millions of kalpas, it is difficult even to hear the name of a Buddha.
The father should give rise to deep, pure faith toward the Buddha.
If one can even utter the Buddha’s name, such a person is already difficult to encounter;
how much more so to behold the Buddha’s own body! Therefore, the father should have faith.
Just as the Guide described, manifesting immeasurable supernatural powers and emitting immeasurable rays of light— this person has now arrived.
As previously stated, nayutas of lands have been shaken.
Immeasurable sons of the Buddhas have come here out of compassion for the multitudes.
Having arrived from various directions in the ten quarters, they are as difficult to overcome as lions;
gods, humans, nāgas, and others rejoice and rain down a multitude of flowers.

At that time, the merchant’s daughter, Śrīprabhā, saw the great trembling of the earth and the great supernormal power of a vast, brilliant radiance of various distinct colors. Having seen this, she was filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for gladness. Taking a basket filled with various flowers, she quickly went to her father’s side, joined her palms, and with a heart of great faith and great joy, addressed her father in verse:
“Father, you now place your trust in non-Buddhists; This mind is most grievous.
Falling into the midst of the wicked and evil, You constantly lack faith in the Buddha-dharma.”
They push others into evil realms and block the path to the good;
these who are ever unsubdued lose the benefits of the Buddha’s merit.
The Buddha is like the udumbara flower; even if one were to practice for hundreds of thousands of eons, [he would not appear].
It is always difficult even to hear his name, let alone to be able to see him.
Now that your father has placed faith in a non-Buddhist path, you have given rise to a dual mind in inviting the Buddha;
yet now that you have already heard his name and seen him, you ought not to harbor evil thoughts.
Do not give rise to turbid thoughts, nor any intent to harm;
always cultivate pure faith and rejoice in the Buddha.
The Buddha’s spiritual power is inconceivable, universally covering the realms of the ten directions.
The Buddha’s disciples with moon-like faces, along with the nāgas, devas, yakṣas, and others—
all paid him their respects; with hearts of faith,
they bowed in reverence to the Buddha and scattered māndārava flowers over the Buddha and the great assembly.
The disciples of the Buddha rejoice, while the minds of the heterodox throng are deluded and turbid;
the Buddha-sun eclipses the heretics, just as the sun outshines the glow of fireflies.
This Great Being of supreme vows bows before the Buddha, who is difficult to behold.
I see immeasurable retinues surrounding the Honored One Śākyamuni;
with supreme wisdom and pure knowledge, he cannot be defeated by non-Buddhists.
Like clouds that cover and sandalwood incense clouds, they are adorned with all manner of diverse ornaments.

At that time, Candraprabha’s younger brother, the youth Dṛḍhamati, had already in the past made offerings to various buddhas and planted roots of goodness, having purified his brahmacarya under those buddhas.

At that time, the boy saw in a dream the Buddha’s great supernormal power as he descended from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, intending to enter the city of Rājagṛha. As the earth shook violently, he immediately awoke; he put on his robes and adjusted his garments, then hurried to the gate, filled with great joy, and returned to his father’s presence, where he spoke these verses:
“In my dream I saw the Buddha; in this single instant, from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the greatest of mountain peaks, he descended.”
With inconceivable great power, surrounded by a host of bodhisattvas who have each come from various lands, they know the distinctions of the dharma-realm.
Each and every bodhisattva is surrounded by an immeasurable multitude.
Dwelling in each of those lands, his name cannot be heard.
A great wise Bodhisattva named Vimalaprabha,
a guide for all Buddhas, holds a parasol made of the seven precious jewels.
He utters wondrous sounds, which all who hear delight in;
he is likewise able to pervade the immeasurable lands of the ten directions.
I behold that World-Honored One, who is able to destroy all strife and contention.
Having awakened from the dream, he immediately went to his father’s place and said:
"Father, you should now believe in the Buddha; abandon the foolish non-Buddhists who corrupt the human mind;
you ought to distance yourself from them quickly."
Even if there were fires filling the worlds throughout the ten directions,
they could not burn the Buddha’s robe, much less the Tathāgata’s body;
even if there were various poisonous drugs filling hundreds of thousands of lands, [they could not harm him].
One does not harm the disciples of the Buddha, much less the Tathāgata himself.
Among all poisons, the Buddha is foremost in being free from them;
by not dwelling upon poison, it naturally dissipates—how much more so when one does not even dwell upon it? Thus, it is utterly extinguished.
The Omniscient One, well-tamed, has now come to the city of Rājagṛha;
these inconceivable Bodhisattvas have all reached the further shore.
Throughout all three periods of time, their forms may be heard of or seen.
He is able to bestow peace and security upon all; therefore, Father, you should believe this.
His coming is not in vain; Father, you ought to make offerings to him.
The Buddha emits immeasurable light, which can dispel these false darknesses.
This light illuminates devas and humans, asuras, nāgas, and yakṣas, along with all their retinues; for all who see it, it is not in vain.
All the hot hells are entirely cooled.
The sentient beings within the hells, their heat removed, rejoice with hearts full of joy.
The Brahmā gods and the celestial lords all emit fragrant clouds from their bodies;
like canopies of variegated silks, they adorn the void of space.
Coming here with an unimpeded mind, like the supreme guide Nāgaśūra,
he is able to raise clouds of renunciation and bestow a rain of various kinds of jewels,
exquisite jeweled necklaces, sandalwood, and parasols.
Pervading the void of space and the worlds of the ten directions,
they come here able to discern all things; having reached the further shore through supernormal powers,
they know every variety of distinction and are able to praise all Buddhas.
Innumerable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of devas, as well as the eminent people of this city,
having heard the Buddha’s great and famous name, have all come to where the Buddha is.
The elephants let out cries of joy, and the lions do likewise.
Even the wild leaders of the herds of oxen let out such cries;
when animals hear the name of the Buddha, they all give rise to a heart of joy.
Since humans are superior to these fathers, why do you not believe?
Tens of millions of nayutas of immeasurable musical instruments,
along with precious necklaces and vessels, resounded spontaneously without being struck.
Immeasurable kinds of animals [gathered] before the Peerless One of Ten Powers.
Abandoning the poisonous mind, one gives rise to joyful and pure faith;
able to destroy the demons of strife, one is tamed and enters great quiescence.
Reaching the further shore through patience, one’s heart of loving-kindness is vast and compassionate.
With compassion reaching the further shore, Able to rescue all sentient beings,
Practicing various forms of giving, And able to give rise to the bodhicitta—
Father, you should believe in Śākyamuni, Who has transcended the worldly shore.
Able to radiate light throughout the ten directions, Sentient beings are freed from the eight difficulties;
Possessing such manifold spiritual powers, Inconceivable across the three periods of time,
Wandering like a lion, With wisdom reaching the further shore.
His wisdom abides like Mount Sumeru, constantly radiating precious light.
Surrounded by the assembly of the Buddha’s sons before and behind him,
he manifests various supernormal powers as he arrives at the city of Rājagṛha.
Adorned and embellished with various kinds of exquisite jewels,
the hosts of devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, along with hundreds of billions of asuras,
join their palms in reverent worship to the Honored One Śākyamuni.
The Tamer now stands at the gate; when his feet step upon the threshold,
the blind shall see forms, the deaf shall hear sounds,
the suffering shall find peace and joy, and the sick shall be healed.
Those suffering the pains of pregnancy and childbirth shall safely escape their distress;
all shall obtain precious treasuries, and the poor shall attain abundance.
Through the pure supernatural powers of the Buddha, all shall be filled with joy.
All the ground within the city is entirely filled with various jewels,
adorned with lovely treasures whose colors are most majestic and radiant;
as he walks through the streets in his disciplined composure, Father, you should rise to welcome him.
In the corridors and multi-storied pavilions, men and women were all gathered;
with garments filled with fragrant flowers and various precious necklaces,
they scattered them over Śākyamuni with pure and joyful hearts.
The king was named Śreṇika; accompanied by sixty thousand court ladies, each holding various kinds of precious jewels, he made offerings to the Tathāgata.
He presented robes, exquisite jeweled necklaces, as well as various wonderful incenses and flowers.
They also gave rise to a heart of joy and scattered [flowers] over the Buddha.
Wise people filled the streets; with faith and delight seeking merit, their hearts leaped with joy as they prostrated before the World-Honored One, the Buddha.
The Buddha comes from the street, and hundreds of billions of sentient beings join their palms in joy; all of them prostrate,
reaching down through all worlds and up as far as the Peak of Existence.
In all lands throughout the ten directions, Filled with assemblies of devas and humans,
Various kinds of beings Make offerings to the Tathāgata;
All are filled with joy, And with pure hearts, they pay homage to the Buddha.
The Tīrthika Vaiśeṣika teacher prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One;
with a heart of supreme joy and most excellent pure faith, he joined his palms and praised the Buddha: "Excellent! The Buddha has appeared in the world."
Possessing great wisdom and all-encompassing knowledge, he has already reached the further shore.
Father, you should give rise to joy; go together with him to the Tathāgata’s abode, take excellent precious garments, and offer them as worship to the Tathāgata.
Having eliminated doubt and the mind of jealousy, as well as all evil views, and having faith that the Buddha is supreme in the world, I prostrate to the King of Munis.
Father, you should now know: he is the one who tames sentient beings.
He is able to protect and shelter all sentient beings,
and can utterly extinguish every sinful thought; such a Great Guide,
out of compassion for his father, has now come to stand outside the gate.
The fire pit shall extinguish itself of its own accord, and various lotuses shall emerge:
the utpala, kumuda, padma, and puṇḍarīka.
The devas and worldlings, along with their retinues of nāgas and spirits, [shall behold this].
Various kinds of flower fragrances were scattered, filling the earth on all sides.
This Guide, the Banner of Wisdom, whose majestic radiance is difficult to behold,
possesses the knowledge and vision of omniscience and has reached the further shore.
Knowing the mental karma of the three periods of time and their distinctions as superior, middling, or inferior, Father,
you should rejoice with faith. That which is difficult to see and difficult to hear—
throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas— you have practiced austerities for the sake of the multitude.
Endowed with all virtues, He has forever eliminated all transgressions.
For those who wish to cultivate meritorious deeds, This field of merit is most supreme;
Out of compassion for sentient beings, He manifests his presence in the world.
Not for the sake of seeking food or clothing, nor to display his own wisdom,
but solely out of great compassion and pity for his father, he has come.
Knowing that his father had conceived evil thoughts and was shrouded by those wrong views, [he approached].
Desiring to bring about their liberation, he causes them to abandon the karma of killing.
Toward all sentient beings, the Buddha is entirely equal;
he has no thought of discrimination, nor does he harbor notions of enemy or kin.
The Tathāgata’s true wisdom is forever free from all deceit and crookedness;
father, you should give rise to faith and respect him with prostrations.
The Buddha-jewel is the most excellent in the world, having completely cast out all evil views.
The Father can inspire joyful faith, And the net of doubt is utterly removed.
Because of faith in the Tathāgata, One does not fall into the various evil realms.
The Buddha can purify the five faculties; One should swiftly pay him homage.
The Great Teacher of the three periods of time, surrounded by a multitude of Buddha-sons,
dwells within various stages, practicing with unobstructed wisdom.
These sons of the All-Knowing One surround and illuminate the Tathāgata.
Like the sun eclipsing all the stars, he is therefore worthy of reverent salutation.
When the father saw the Buddha’s supernatural power— the fire pit filled with water and various lotuses emerging— his heart was filled with great joy.
Having witnessed these various transformations, he looked back at his son Candraprabha and said:
“You are my teacher; out of compassion you have come to be born here.
Because I believed in the non-Buddhist paths, my mind was constantly harboring malice.”
I now respectfully believe in the Buddha and have completely abandoned all wrong views;
this child was a spiritual friend to me, difficult to encounter,
who exhorted me to believe in the Buddha, causing me to give rise to great joy.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, and Maheśvara—
these two great celestial kings— prepared a seat for the Buddha;
eighty thousand koṭis of devas covered the jeweled throne with their robes.
Causing the Omniscient One to sit, he manifested him so that he shone with brilliance.
Having paid homage to the Buddha, the Brahma King held a precious parasol for him,
made of Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with various jewels.
Together with the other devas and their peers, they joined their palms in homage to the Buddha,
scattering hundreds of kinds of various flowers and red sandalwood powder.
Having seen the Buddha, the elder’s heart was filled with great joy.
Eight thousand women attained pure wisdom;
five hundred youths and five hundred maidens,
beholding the Buddha’s supernormal powers, all resolved to attain bodhicitta.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions, nayutas of devaputras,
having witnessed the Buddha’s supernormal powers, attained pure wisdom. The elder,
harboring grief and affliction, felt great shame in his heart.
Even as he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he turned toward the Buddha and confessed:
“This food is mixed with poisonous medicine; I now wish to prepare another offering.
I pray only that the World-Honored Buddha will deign to remain for a short while.”
With a wondrous Brahma-voice, the Tathāgata addressed the elder Guṇapāla:
"The Tathāgata, possessed of all-knowledge, can dispel every poison—
the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the worldly poisons."
The Tathāgata speaks the truth: I have long since abandoned the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the worldly toxins.
Having abandoned these poisons through the pure Dharma, I have distanced myself from all such speech by means of truthful words.
"The three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the worldly poisons—
all these are utterly abandoned by the pure Saṃgha who is free from poison and speaks the truth.
When the Buddha spoke these words, immeasurable devas raised their voices and cried out:
